methodological_rigor.justification: The retrospective single-center design (Section 2.1) is appropriate for a head-to-head comparison of MOLES and MelAInoma, and the authors explicitly state that this cohort was independent of the training set for the MelAInoma algorithm (strength). The analytic plan is competent: Jonckheere–Terpstra for ordered trend, linear and binary logistic regression with Tjur's R², multivariable adjustment, bootstrap internal validation (2000 resamples) with optimism correction, Hosmer–Lemeshow calibration, and a DeLong AUC comparison across imaging modalities (Sections 2.3, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8). Important limitations include small sample (n=86 with only 29 melanomas), no a priori power calculation, no histopathologic ground truth, highly imbalanced MOLES categories (e.g., n=8 in several groups), and critical shared-feature incorporation bias since MOLES scores and the reference diagnosis were produced by the same subspecialty graders using the same multimodal data — the authors acknowledge this (Section 'Strengths and Limitations') but it structurally limits causal inference. No pre-registration or pre-specified analysis plan is reported.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort study using expert multimodal clinical diagnosis as the reference standard (Section 2.1), corresponding to Oxford LoE 2b. The clinical question — triage of pigmented choroidal lesions to reduce unnecessary referrals while identifying small melanomas early — is genuinely relevant to ocular oncology practice, especially given the stated Swedish optometry pathway (Section 1, Discussion). However, the endpoint is diagnostic concordance/association with expert classification rather than a patient-centered outcome (OS, PFS, metastasis), and the translational path remains dependent on prospective, multicenter, non-expert-user validation that the authors acknowledge is still needed. The findings are directly supportive of decision aids rather than practice-changing.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable standard given the retrospective observational cohort design. The manuscript reports most core STROBE items — setting, eligibility criteria, variables, imaging modalities, statistical methods, descriptive characteristics, and effect estimates with confidence intervals — and includes a thoughtful limitations section. Notable omissions include no participant flow diagram, no explicit handling of missing data, no sample size justification, no reporting of blinding of MOLES graders to diagnosis, and no mention of pre-registration. No data-sharing statement, repository, or code availability is reported; the MelAInoma software is referenced as a commercial product (Eyedentity AB), and underlying image data/scores are not deposited, limiting reproducibility to method description alone.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is empirical and incremental: a direct head-to-head comparison between an established manual scoring system (MOLES, refs 20–21) and the authors' previously published MelAInoma algorithm (ref 19) in an independent cohort. The idea of AI-based choroidal lesion classification is not new, and the MelAInoma algorithm itself was reported previously (refs 15, 19); comparable AI approaches for choroidal nevus risk also exist (ref 31). The specific contribution — demonstrating that a single-photo deep learning model performs comparably to multimodal expert MOLES scoring and provides independent information in multivariable models — is a meaningful extension but not conceptually or methodologically transformative. Positioning relative to prior MOLES evaluations (refs 20–24) and prior MelAInoma validations is credible and does not overclaim.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well-organized with a plain-language summary preceding a structured abstract, clear Introduction–Methods–Results–Discussion flow, and informative section subheadings. Terminology is defined (e.g., MOLES features expanded on first use), results are presented with effect sizes and CIs alongside tables and figures referenced in-text, and the Discussion engages seriously with shared-feature incorporation bias and distributional differences between score types. Minor issues include occasional awkward phrasing ('showed substantially improved the fit', Section 3.6), repetitive referencing of the authors' own prior work in both Introduction and Discussion, and a very long limitations paragraph that could be tightened. Overall, publication-quality scientific writing.

key_strengths: Independent test cohort not used for MelAInoma training (Section 2.1), with ≥5-year follow-up required for nevus classification

Competent statistical workflow: Jonckheere–Terpstra trend test, Tjur's R², multivariable logistic regression, bootstrap optimism correction (2000 resamples) with calibration slope 0.89, and DeLong AUC comparison across imaging subgroups
Transparent acknowledgment of shared-feature incorporation bias between MOLES scoring and expert reference diagnosis, which structurally favors MOLES
Clinically relevant question addressing triage of pigmented choroidal lesions in non-expert settings with a plausible deployment pathway
Clear, well-structured writing with a plain-language summary and thoughtful limitations
key_concerns: Small single-center cohort (n=86; 29 melanomas) with no a priori power calculation and imbalanced MOLES category counts limiting stability of estimates
No histopathologic ground truth; reference standard is multimodal expert diagnosis by the same subspecialty graders who assigned MOLES (circularity acknowledged but not resolvable in design)
Incremental novelty — the MelAInoma algorithm and its validations are prior work (refs 15, 19); this is primarily a head-to-head comparison in an existing cohort
Subgroup AUC comparisons by imaging modality were underpowered (overlapping CIs; DeLong p=0.42 and 0.48) yet are interpreted as supporting stability
No data/code availability statement, no pre-registration, and incomplete STROBE adherence (no flow diagram, no blinding reported)
Generalizability limited to the Swedish referral context and the two camera systems used
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a methodologically competent but incremental comparison study with real design limitations (circular reference standard, small single-center cohort, no histopathology). It fits a mid-tier specialty oncology or imaging journal (Tier 3) with minor revisions to strengthen reporting (STROBE flow, data/code availability, clarification of blinding) and to temper comparative claims given overlapping subgroup CIs.
